stops.name: Rosario: Entre Ríos 480, birthplace
stops.campa: In a rented apartment on Calle Entre Ríos, Ernesto Guevara de la Serna is born to Ernesto Guevara Lynch and Celia de la Serna, aristocrats of restless blood: Irish rebels and Spanish viceroys in the line. The family is only passing through Rosario, bound downriver; the child of the journey is born mid-journey. His father will say later that in his son's veins flowed the blood of Irish rebels, and that Ernesto was born with it already in revolt. The storm of the century's second half enters the world quietly, wrapped against the river damp.

stops.name: Caraguataí, Misiones, the yerba mate plantation
stops.campa: The family lives on the wild bank of the Alto Paraná, where the father plants yerba mate and the jungle presses in: snakes, red earth, the river running like a green god past the landing. The infant Ernesto is carried through plantations where mensú laborers work off debts they can never pay; his mother swims the dangerous river while he watches from the bank. The first landscape of his life is the frontier itself: heat, insects, the poor bent over the bitter leaf that Argentina drinks.

stops.name: San Isidro, Buenos Aires, the first asthma attack
stops.campa: On the second of May his mother takes the two-year-old swimming at the club on a cold autumn morning, and that night the child begins to drown in air. The asthma arrives like a lifelong angel of contradiction: the disease that will chain him to inhalers and cortisone is the same one that forges the will of iron. The doctors say the boy may not live a normal life. The family begins its wandering in search of breathable air, and the boy begins his apprenticeship in fighting his own body every single night.

stops.name: Alta Gracia, Córdoba, Villa Nydia
stops.campa: For the boy's lungs the family climbs to the dry hill air of Alta Gracia and settles at Villa Nydia. Here the legend of the sickly child who refuses to be sick is written: between attacks he cannot walk to school, so Celia teaches him to read in bed among her books; between books he hurls himself at football, golf, and fistfights with the sons of quarry workers and caddies, the poor boys he prefers. Spanish Republican exiles pass through the parlor with the smell of a lost war. The asthma dictates the rhythm; the will dictates everything else.

stops.name: Córdoba, Colegio Deán Funes, meeting Alberto Granado
stops.campa: The family moves down to Córdoba city and Ernesto enters the Deán Funes secondary school. On the rugby pitch of Estudiantes he throws his wheezing body into the scrum, pausing at the touchline for his inhaler, and earns the name Fuser: Furibundo Serna, the furious one. The team's trainer is a short, laughing biochemistry student named Alberto Granado, six years older, keeper of a motorcycle and of large ideas. The friendship that will drive across a continent is founded here, between scrums, over books by Freud, Neruda and Verne.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Faculty of Medicine
stops.campa: Celia's cancer and the family's move bring Ernesto to Buenos Aires, where he enrolls in medicine at the university on Calle Paraguay. He works in Dr. Pisani's allergy clinic, hunting his own disease down the microscope, half-patient and half-researcher. He reads omnivorously, plays chess, keeps a handwritten philosophical dictionary, and takes jobs and journeys whenever the city grows too small. The examiners know him as brilliant and absent by turns; the road already has more authority over him than the lecture hall.
stops.quote: When I began to study medicine... I dreamed of becoming a famous researcher, of working tirelessly to achieve something that could truly be placed at the disposal of humanity.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, speech 'On Revolutionary Medicine', Havana, 19 August 1960 (recalling his student years)

stops.name: San Francisco del Chañar: the leprosarium, on the motorized bicycle
stops.campa: On the first of January 1950 the medical student pedals out of Buenos Aires alone on a bicycle fitted with a tiny Cucciolo motor, bound for the north, four thousand five hundred kilometers through twelve provinces. He climbs to the leprosarium of San Francisco del Chañar where Alberto Granado now works, and for the first time sits long hours with lepers, learning that the sick want a hand shaken without gloves more than they want pity. The manufacturer of the little motor will run his photograph as an advertisement: the first published image of the traveler.

stops.name: Salta, the hospital and the soul of a people
stops.campa: At the northern apex of the ride he sleeps in police stations and hospital corridors, taking Argentina in through the skin: cane cutters of Tucumán, the dispossessed of the dry Chaco edge, vagabonds who share fire and mate. In Salta the hospital staff ask the returning cyclist what he has seen, and he understands that he has not traveled the way tourists travel. He writes it down in the notebook, the first formulation of the creed: the country is read in its sick, its prisoners, its anxious passersby, not in its monuments.
stops.quote: I am not nourished by the same things as tourists... the soul of a people is reflected in the sick of its hospitals, the inmates of its police stations, the anxious passerby one talks to.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, 1950 travel notebook, cited in Anderson's biography

stops.name: Buenos Aires, departure on La Poderosa II
stops.campa: On the fourth of January, Ernesto, twenty-three, and Alberto Granado, twenty-nine, roar out of Buenos Aires on La Poderosa II, Alberto's overloaded 1939 Norton 500: the Mighty One, named with irony and love. The plan is continental and absurd: the whole spine of Latin America, ending at a leprosarium on the Amazon. Celia weeps at the departure. The bike carries a tent, a revolver, a grill, and two futures. Nine symbolic months of gestation begin; what will be born at the end is not the same young man who leaves.
stops.quote: This is not a story of heroic feats... it is a glimpse of two lives running parallel for a time, with similar hopes and convergent dreams.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, preface ('So we understand each other')

stops.name: Miramar, Chichina by the sea
stops.campa: The road bends first toward love. At the resort of Miramar, María del Carmen 'Chichina' Ferreyra, heiress of Córdoba aristocracy, summers with her disapproving family, and two planned days stretch to eight. Ernesto carries her gift, a gold bracelet as amulet, and leaves her his dog, ominously named Comeback. On the dunes the two futures pull against each other: the estancia and the road. The sea witnesses the wager. When La Poderosa finally points south again, something has already been decided that neither of them says aloud.

stops.name: Bahía Blanca, last city of the pampa
stops.campa: The travelers rest with friends in Bahía Blanca, the last big town before the desert of the south, patching the Norton and their finances. Leaving, Ernesto rides feverish and half-delirious into the dunes of Médanos, where the heavy bike bucks and falls again and again in the loose sand; he counts the spills like a boxer counting knockdowns. Fever forces him into bed. The journey is teaching its first lesson: the continent is not scenery, it is an adversary, and it will be crossed on its own terms.

stops.name: Choele Choel, fever in the Río Negro valley
stops.campa: Burning with flu, Ernesto is carried to the small regional hospital at Choele Choel on the Río Negro, where penicillin and days of sleep pull him back. Alberto charms the doctors; the patient, restless, writes. In the irrigated valley the two future leprologists are treated as colleagues, given beds and meals in exchange for medical talk. It is the journey's rhythm now: break down, be rescued by the kindness of ordinary Argentines, repay in stories, roll on. The Norton waits outside like a tethered animal.
